source.title: Open fire in hearth grate at The Black Horse Inn, Nuthurst, West Sussex.jpg

images.alt: Logs burning in an open brick hearth, the fire lighting the grate from within.
images.caption: A hearth is the oldest picture of a house that is warm enough to sit still in — which is the kind of reading this site is for.

credit.title: Open fire in a hearth grate
credit.creator: Simon Carey

source.title: Codex Sinaiticus.jpg

images.alt: A sheet of the Codex Sinaiticus, four columns of Greek uncial script on parchment.
images.caption: The writing on this site is new. The text it is about is not: a fourth-century copy of the Greek Bible, still readable.

source.title: Long Room Interior, Trinity College Dublin, Ireland - Diliff.jpg

images.alt: The Long Room of Trinity College Dublin, a barrel-vaulted gallery of old books in two storeys.
images.caption: A room built to keep books in reach of anyone who walks in — the same job a chapter study page is trying to do.

credit.title: The Long Room, Trinity College Dublin
credit.creator: David Iliff

source.title: Gutenberg Bible, Lenox Copy, New York Public Library, 2009. Pic 01.jpg

images.alt: An open spread of a Gutenberg Bible, blackletter columns on cream paper in a library case.
images.caption: Topics on this site are not a verse index. They are an argument, the way a printed Bible is an argument bound in order.

source.title: Epistolae Pauli cum glossa ordinaria. - btv1b8426047w (226 of 395).jpg

images.alt: A medieval manuscript of Paul with the biblical text in a centre column and commentary packed into the margins.
images.caption: Hard questions have always been answered in the margins of the passage, not instead of it.

credit.title: Pauline epistles with the Glossa ordinaria
credit.creator: Unknown scribes

source.title: Michelangelo - Creation of Adam (cropped).jpg

images.alt: Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam: two hands reaching across a gap, almost touching.
images.caption: The chapter’s claim in one gesture: people are made, on purpose, and the gap between maker and made does not close itself.

source.title: John Martin - The Deluge - Google Art Project.jpg

images.alt: John Martin’s The Deluge: a dark sky over heaving water, tiny figures clinging to rock.
images.caption: Genesis 6 is not a children’s-ark picture. Martin painted the water as something that unmakes a world.

source.title: "The good Shepherd" mosaic - Mausoleum of Galla Placidia.jpg

images.alt: A fifth-century mosaic of a young shepherd in a gold landscape, sheep at his feet, a cross-staff in his hand.
images.caption: Christians put Psalm 23 on the walls of tombs: not a rural postcard, but a claim that the shepherd does not leave the valley.

source.title: Late Winter Sunrise on Lake Okanagan.JPG

images.alt: Pale winter sunrise reflecting on a still lake, light coming up behind dark hills.
images.caption: “The Lord is my light” is not a metaphor for cheerfulness. It is a claim that the dark does not get the last word.

credit.title: Late winter sunrise on Lake Okanagan
credit.creator: Wing-Chi Poon

source.title: Judean desert004.jpg

images.alt: Bare limestone hills of the Judean desert under a hard sky, no green in sight.
images.caption: Psalm 28 calls God a rock while the poet is still shouting into silence. The landscape here is the kind of place that makes that prayer make sense.

source.title: Luttichuys, Isaac - Still Life with Bread and Wine Glass - 17th c.jpg

images.alt: A seventeenth-century still life: a loaf of bread, a glass of wine, and a knife on a wooden table.
images.caption: “Taste and see” is an invitation to something as ordinary as bread, not a slogan about positive thinking.

credit.title: Still Life with Bread and Wine Glass
credit.creator: Isaac Luttichuys

source.title: Dülmen, Umland, Sonnenaufgang -- 2012 -- 8084.jpg

images.alt: A river winding through fields at sunrise, mist lying low along the water.
images.caption: The psalm’s river is not scenery. It is the thing that keeps a city alive while the rest of the earth is giving way.

source.title: Schnorr von Carolsfeld Bibel in Bildern 1860 102.png

images.alt: A woodcut of the prophet Nathan confronting King David, who covers his face.
images.caption: Psalm 51 is what David says after Nathan has said “You are the man.” The engraving keeps that order: first the charge, then the prayer.

source.title: ISR-2016-Masada 04.jpg

images.alt: The rock fortress of Masada seen from below, a flat-topped crag above the desert.
images.caption: Psalm 91 talks about shelter the way a fortress talks about it: not that danger is imaginary, but that there is a place it does not own.

source.title: Mount Hermon View.jpg

images.alt: Snow-capped Mount Hermon rising over a wide valley, hills receding into haze.
images.caption: “I lift up my eyes to the hills” is the start of a question, not a nature lyric: the help does not come from the hills themselves.

source.title: ALMA and a Starry Night.jpg

images.alt: The Milky Way over the ALMA antennas on a high plateau, the sky dense with stars.
images.caption: Psalm 139’s night is not empty. It is the place the psalmist says you still cannot hide.

source.title: Bloch-SermonOnTheMount.jpg

images.alt: Carl Bloch’s Sermon on the Mount: Jesus seated on a hillside, a crowd gathered on the grass below him.
images.caption: Matthew 5 is a sermon delivered to people sitting on a hill, not a poster of virtues. Bloch painted the crowd as well as the speaker.

source.title: Lilium candidum in Wadi Kelah 1.jpg

images.alt: White Madonna lilies growing on a rocky slope, trumpets open toward the light.
images.caption: “Consider the lilies” is an argument about anxiety, made from a flower that does not farm and is still dressed.

source.title: Henry Ossawa Tanner - Nicodemus coming to Christ.jpg

images.alt: Henry Ossawa Tanner’s Nicodemus visiting Jesus at night, two figures in a dim courtyard, a lantern between them.
images.caption: John 3 happens after dark, on purpose. Tanner painted the lantern, not a spotlight: this is a conversation a Pharisee would rather not have in public.

source.title: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) - The Last Supper (1495-1498).jpg

images.alt: Leonardo’s Last Supper: Jesus at the centre of a long table, the disciples reacting around him.
images.caption: John 14 is spoken at this table, after the meal has already turned. The room is the point: “In my Father’s house” is said by someone about to leave it.

source.title: John Martin - Joshua Commanding the Sun to Stand Still - Google Art Project.jpg

images.alt: John Martin’s Joshua commanding the sun: a vast army under a sky split by light, the sun halted above the field.
images.caption: Joshua 1 is the charge before any of that happens: be strong, because the work in front of you is larger than you.

credit.title: Joshua Commanding the Sun to Stand Still
credit.creator: John Martin

source.title: Ishtar Gate at Berlin Museum.jpg

images.alt: The reconstructed Ishtar Gate: glazed blue brick, bulls and dragons in relief, under a museum roof.
images.caption: Jeremiah 29 is a letter to people living under this kind of power, told to unpack and plant gardens rather than wait for a quick rescue.

source.title: Aerial view of the Judean Desert (near Masada), Israel 03.jpg

images.alt: An aerial view of the Judean desert: ridged limestone, dry wadis, almost no vegetation.
images.caption: Isaiah 41 promises rivers on this kind of ground. The promise is only as large as the dryness it names.

source.title: Molnár Ábrahám kiköltözése 1850.jpg

images.alt: József Molnár’s painting of Abraham’s household on the move: tents, camels, and a long road under a wide sky.
images.caption: Hebrews 11 is a list of people who left before they arrived. Abraham is first in that line because he packed while the destination was still only a promise.

images.alt: A Greek bronze mirror of the fifth century BCE, the disc held up by a small draped figure.
images.caption: James says a person who hears the word and does not do it is like someone who looks in a mirror and walks away having forgotten the face.

credit.title: Bronze mirror with a support in the form of a draped woman
credit.creator: Unknown Greek bronzeworker

source.title: John Martin - The Plains of Heaven - Google Art Project.jpg

images.alt: John Martin’s Plains of Heaven: a luminous lake and distant mountains under a vast, crowded sky.
images.caption: Revelation 21 is not an escape from earth. Martin painted a world, not a cloud: the claim is that the holy city comes down.

source.title: Оld Olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane, 05.jpg

images.alt: Ancient olive trees in Gethsemane, thick twisted trunks and silver leaves against stone.
images.caption: Romans 8 is about a life the Spirit keeps going. Olive trees of this age are the nearest plant-picture of that: still alive after more winters than anyone present remembers.

credit.title: Old olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane
credit.creator: Kristián Slovák

source.title: P46.jpg

images.alt: A leaf of Papyrus 46, early Greek text of Paul written in a compact book hand.
images.caption: Romans 12 is “therefore”: after eleven chapters of argument, the letter turns to what a body of people is for. This is an early copy of that turn.

credit.title: Papyrus 46
credit.creator: Unknown scribe
credit.holder: University of Michigan / Chester Beatty Library

source.title: Van Dyck - Charity.jpg

images.alt: Van Dyck’s Charity: a woman gathering children against her, a picture of caritas rather than romance.
images.caption: Paul’s “love” in this chapter is caritas — the kind that stays when the gifts run out — not the feeling a wedding reading usually means.

source.title: Winter in Trossachs, Scotland.jpg

images.alt: A winter valley in the Trossachs: bare trees, snow on the hills, a season that has clearly arrived.
images.caption: Ecclesiastes 3 does not say every season is pleasant. It says each one has a time, including the ones that look like nothing is growing.

images.alt: A bronze Corinthian helmet, the face-opening a dark T in a surface that once took blows.
images.caption: Ephesians 6 borrows armour because the letter thinks the Christian life is a fight. The pieces named are real pieces, not a costume.

credit.title: Bronze helmet of the Corinthian type
credit.creator: Unknown Greek bronzeworker

source.title: Banquet Still Life, Adriaen van Utrecht, 1644 - Rijksmuseum.jpg

images.alt: A piled still life of fruit, bread, and game, painted as abundance that will not last.
images.caption: The fruit of the Spirit is not a still life. Van Utrecht’s table shows what fruit looks like when it is only produce: impressive, and already on the way to rotting.

source.title: The Apostle Paul - Rembrandt.jpg

images.alt: Rembrandt’s Apostle Paul: an old man in a dark room, a manuscript on the table, light on his face.
images.caption: Philippians 4’s “do not be anxious” is written from confinement. Rembrandt painted Paul with the letter, not with a halo.

source.title: Aleppo Codex (Deut).jpg

images.alt: A page of the Aleppo Codex, Hebrew written in a precise masoretic hand with vowel points.
images.caption: Proverbs 3 is wisdom meant to be copied, not invented on the spot. This is what that kind of copying looked like when it was done with care.

source.title: Field of Flax - geograph.org.uk - 282010.jpg

images.alt: A field of blue flax in flower, low plants stretching to a hedge under an ordinary sky.
images.caption: Proverbs 31’s woman works in flax and wool. The chapter is about skill and provision, not a personality type, and flax is the plant it names.

source.title: Ivan Aivazovsky - Ship in the Stormy Sea.jpg

images.alt: An Aivazovsky seascape: a small ship heeled over in a heavy sea under a torn sky.
images.caption: The Bible’s anxiety passages are written for weather like this, not for a calm that has already arrived.

source.title: Caspar David Friedrich Paysage de Riesengebirge avec la brume montante.jpg

images.alt: A Friedrich landscape: distant ridges fading into rising mist, no figure in the foreground.
images.caption: Some psalms sound like this weather — not theatrical despair, just a view in which the path is hard to see.

source.title: Port and lighthouse overnight storm with lightning in Port-la-Nouvelle.jpg

images.alt: Lightning striking over a harbour at night, a lighthouse and the water lit for an instant.
images.caption: Fear in Scripture is often this sudden: a sky that was weather and is now a threat. The verses about it do not pretend the storm is imaginary.

source.title: Calm waters, Sea of Galilee 0833 (508209962).jpg

images.alt: The Sea of Galilee on a still day, pale hills across a barely ruffled surface.
images.caption: Biblical peace is not the absence of a lake that can storm. It is what is said to hold when the water has a history of not staying like this.

source.title: Sunrise Reflections - Lake Louise, Alberta, Canada.jpg

images.alt: Sunrise on Lake Louise: pink light on snow peaks, the water holding a clear reflection.
images.caption: Hope in the Bible is not optimism about the weather. It is waiting for a light you cannot yet walk by — and this is what the waiting is for.

source.title: Winter in der Rhön.jpg

images.alt: A winter hillside of bare trees and snow, the colour gone out of the ground.
images.caption: Grief in Scripture is allowed to look like a season that has stopped producing. The verses do not skip to spring.

source.title: Easy Access Path, High Beach, Essex, England 2.jpg

images.alt: A pale path running through a wood, trees on both sides, nobody on the track.
images.caption: The lonely psalms are walked, not posed. A path with no one else on it is the honest picture.

source.title: Henri Horace Roland de la Porte (c.1724-1793) - Still Life with Bread and Wine - YORAG , 764 - York Art Gallery.jpg

images.alt: A still life of bread and wine on a table, painted without a human figure in the frame.
images.caption: Biblical love is closer to a shared table than to a feeling. Bread and wine are what the text keeps putting in people’s hands.

credit.title: Still Life with Bread and Wine
credit.creator: Henri Horace Roland de la Porte

source.title: Albrecht Dürer - Praying Hands, 1508 - Google Art Project.jpg

images.alt: Dürer’s study of two praying hands, the sleeves bunched, the fingers pressed together.
images.caption: Prayer in the Bible is often this unadorned: hands, and nothing else in the picture to explain them.

source.title: Huseifa hoard - Tyrian shekel (1).JPG

images.alt: A silver Tyrian shekel, the kind of coin that circulated in the first-century Levant.
images.caption: When the Gospels mention money they mean a real coin, with a weight and a stamp, not an abstraction called “wealth.”

credit.title: Tyrian shekel from the Huseifa hoard
credit.creator: Hanay

source.title: Les Noces de Cana - Paolo Veronese - Musée du Louvre Peintures INV 142 ; MR 384.jpg

images.alt: Veronese’s Wedding at Cana: a crowded feast, musicians, and jars in a vast architectural setting.
images.caption: The one wedding Jesus attends in the Gospels is a feast that runs out of wine. Marriage in Scripture is public, costly, and in need of help.

source.title: Pieter Aertsen Peasants by the Hearth.jpg

images.alt: Aertsen’s peasants gathered by a hearth: a household at work and rest in a single room.
images.caption: Biblical family is a household, not a portrait studio: people who share a fire, work, and the next meal.

credit.title: Peasants by the Hearth
credit.creator: Pieter Aertsen
credit.holder: Museum Mayer van den Bergh, Antwerp

source.title: Cuneiform tablet with a small second tablet- private letter MET DP-13441-020.jpg

images.alt: A clay cuneiform letter, the signs pressed into the tablet while it was still soft.
images.caption: Deuteronomy tells parents to talk about these words at home and on the road. The oldest way to send a word that far is to press it into something that keeps.

source.title: Sinapis alba subsp. mairei kz03.jpg

images.alt: A mustard plant in flower, small yellow blooms on a branching green stem.
images.caption: Jesus compared faith to a mustard seed because the plant is ordinary and then suddenly not. This is the plant, not a jewel.

source.title: Rembrandt Harmensz van Rijn - Return of the Prodigal Son - Google Art Project.jpg

images.alt: Rembrandt’s Return of the Prodigal Son: the father gathering the kneeling son, the older brother looking on.
images.caption: Forgiveness in the Gospels has a body in it. Rembrandt painted the father’s hands, not a slogan.

credit.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
credit.creator: Rembrandt
credit.holder: The State Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg

source.title: Cima da Conegliano - David and Jonathan - WGA04912.jpg

images.alt: Cima da Conegliano’s David and Jonathan: two young men in a landscape, one holding Goliath’s head, the covenant between them implied in how they stand.
images.caption: The Bible’s strongest picture of friendship is a covenant, not a mood: David and Jonathan bound to each other at a cost.

source.title: Pieter Bruegel the Elder- The Harvesters - Google Art Project.jpg

images.alt: Bruegel’s Harvesters: a wheat field being cut, some workers eating in the shade, a village beyond.
images.caption: Thanksgiving in Scripture is usually for bread that someone had to cut. Bruegel painted the work inside the thanks.

source.title: Roman medical instruments found in Novae, Bulgaria.jpg

images.alt: A set of Roman bronze medical instruments laid out, probes and blades darkened with age.
images.caption: The Gospels’ healings happen in a world that already had doctors and tools. The pages that collect those verses should not pretend otherwise.

source.title: Wooden hourglass 3.jpg

images.alt: A wooden hourglass standing on a table, sand collected in the lower bulb.
images.caption: Patience in the Bible is time you do not control. An hourglass is honest about that in a way a slogan is not.

source.title: Israel-2013-Aerial 21-Masada.jpg

images.alt: An aerial view of Masada: the plateau fortress, the ramp, and the desert dropping away on every side.
images.caption: “God is a fortress” is a metaphor borrowed from places like this: high, costly to take, and built because the plain was not safe.

source.title: Deelerwoud, 09-05-2024 (d.j.b.) 16.jpg

images.alt: A large oak in leaf, the trunk thick, the crown filling the frame.
images.caption: The Bible’s pictures of strength are living things that have lasted — trees, rocks, a remnant — not a flexed pose.

source.title: JudeanDesert.jpg

images.alt: The Judean desert in hard light: pale ground, a few shrubs, hills going back to a dry horizon.
images.caption: Jesus’ temptation is set in a wilderness like this, not in a shop. The first tests in the Gospels happen where there is nothing to eat.

source.title: Anchor at Ferguson Marine - geograph.org.uk - 5204496.jpg

images.alt: A heavy ship’s anchor standing on a quay, chain and flukes at rest.
images.caption: Hebrews calls hope an anchor. The point of the picture is weight, not decoration: something that holds when the water does not.

source.title: Psalms Scroll.jpg

images.alt: The Psalms Scroll from Qumran, Hebrew columns on darkened parchment.
images.caption: Biblical wisdom is a text you copy and return to, not a personality trait. This is what that copying looked like two thousand years ago.

source.title: Carpenter-tools Beveled-edge-chisel-two-angle-gauges-and-carpenters-pencil-01.jpg

images.alt: A carpenter’s chisel, angle gauges, and pencil laid on a wooden bench.
images.caption: The Gospels’ word for Joseph is craftsman. Work in Scripture is tools and a trade, not a branding exercise.

source.title: Allentown PA, Muhlenberg College Ms Theol. Pap. 3 (Papyrus 21) recto Matthew 12, 24-26.jpg

images.alt: Papyrus 21, a fragment of Matthew 12, the chapter that names blasphemy against the Spirit.
images.caption: The unforgivable sin is a sentence in Matthew 12, not a riddle floating free of it. This is an early copy of that page.

images.alt: A Mesopotamian cylinder seal engraved with a cultic scene, made to roll an image into clay.
images.caption: Leviticus 19 is about marks made in a world that already inscribed stone, clay, and skin. The question is which marks, and for whom.

images.alt: A Roman glass cinerary urn with its lid, made to hold what fire left of a body.
images.caption: Cremation is not a modern invention the Bible never met. Rome put ashes in jars like this while the church was learning how to bury its dead.

source.title: Pieter Bruegel the Elder - The Fall of the Rebel Angels - Google Art Project.jpg

images.alt: Bruegel’s Fall of the Rebel Angels: a swarm of hybrid creatures tumbling out of heaven under Michael’s assault.
images.caption: Genesis 6’s “sons of God” and the Nephilim have been read as a fall of angels for a very long time. Bruegel painted that reading; the page has to argue with it, not decorate it.

credit.title: The Fall of the Rebel Angels
credit.creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
credit.holder: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium

source.title: Figures God took Enoch.jpg

images.alt: A historical illustration of Enoch being taken, a rare picture of the Genesis 5–6 world the “sons of God” debate sits inside.
images.caption: The “sons of God” question lives next door to Enoch, who walked with God and was not. The page has to start in that neighbourhood of Genesis, not in a later war in heaven.
